title: Fetal Heart-Rate Variability: Read the Signal in Context
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Baseline fetal heart-rate variability reflects beat-to-beat fluctuation and is interpreted with baseline rate, accelerations, decelerations, contractions, medications, gestational context, and maternal condition. A change in variability is a cue—not a stand-alone diagnosis—and persistent concerning patterns require prompt obstetric escalation.
recognize: Moderate variability is generally reassuring when evaluated with the rest of the tracing.

Minimal or absent variability may be transient with fetal sleep or medications but becomes more concerning when persistent or paired with recurrent decelerations, bradycardia, maternal hypotension, hemorrhage, or other deterioration.
priorities: Review the complete fetal/maternal pattern rather than acting on variability alone.
Escalate persistent concerning variability with abnormal decelerations, bradycardia, tachysystole, maternal instability, or failure to improve after protocol-authorized supportive actions.
assessMonitor: Trend baseline FHR, variability, accelerations/decelerations, contraction frequency, maternal BP/HR/temperature, recent medications, bleeding, membrane status, and response to interventions.
interventions: Maintain accurate monitor placement, reposition as appropriate, correct reversible maternal factors within protocol/orders, and notify the RN/obstetric clinician of concerning changes.
medicationSafety: Opioids, sedatives, magnesium sulfate, oxytocin-related tachysystole, and maternal hypotension can alter the clinical context; medication timing belongs in tracing assessment.
redFlags: Absent/minimal variability with recurrent concerning decelerations
teaching: A tracing is interpreted over time; one brief change does not necessarily mean the fetus is in danger, but persistent abnormal patterns require evaluation.
delegationScope: Independent fetal-tracing interpretation authority varies by state/facility; PN/LVN responsibilities require competency, policy adherence, and prompt reporting of concerning changes.
examTrap: Calling minimal variability fetal hypoxia automatically without checking sleep, medication exposure, decelerations, contractions, and maternal status.
oneLinePearl: Variability is meaningful only inside the whole maternal-fetal pattern.
sourceBasis: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 10, Intrapartum Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring, October 2025

title: Four Stages of Labor: Know What Changes After Birth
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: The first stage runs from labor onset to complete cervical dilation; the second from complete dilation to birth; the third from birth to placental delivery; the immediate recovery period after placental delivery is commonly taught as the fourth stage. Nursing priorities shift rapidly from labor progress and fetal response to hemorrhage, uterine tone, maternal stability, bonding, and newborn transition.
recognize: First-stage care emphasizes contractions, cervical progress, maternal coping, and fetal status; second-stage care adds descent/pushing and birth readiness.
Third- and immediate postpartum-stage care must rapidly recognize uterine atony, retained placenta concern, genital-tract trauma, abnormal bleeding, hypotension, and newborn transition problems.
priorities: Match assessment to the current stage instead of carrying the same checklist through all stages.
After birth, prioritize maternal bleeding, fundal/uterine tone per role and policy, vital signs, pain, bladder status, and newborn transition while supporting bonding when stable.
assessMonitor: Trend maternal vital signs, contractions/labor progress, fetal status before birth, placental delivery status, uterine tone/bleeding, pain, bladder status, and newborn transition after birth.
interventions: Prepare equipment/team for stage transitions, support safe positioning/pushing as directed, assist with active third-stage management per orders/protocol, and escalate postpartum hemorrhage or instability immediately.
medicationSafety: Oxytocin and other uterotonics require indication-specific monitoring and contraindication awareness; PN/LVN administration authority follows state/facility policy.
redFlags: Newborn apnea or poor tone requiring resuscitation
teaching: Birth is not the end of monitoring; the first hours after placental delivery are a critical maternal and newborn observation period.
delegationScope: Diagnosis of labor arrest, management of retained placenta, and obstetric procedural decisions belong to qualified clinicians; PN/LVN role centers monitoring, support, authorized medications/interventions, and escalation.
examTrap: Relaxing surveillance immediately after the baby is born and missing postpartum hemorrhage during placental delivery or early recovery.
oneLinePearl: The priority changes with the stage—and after birth, bleeding and stability move to the front.
sourceBasis: ACOG First and Second Stage Labor Management
